# The Museum of Unfinished Things

The first rule of working at the Museum of Unfinished Things was simple: never read an exhibit label after midnight.

The second was: do not touch anything before dawn.

The third, added in faded blue ink by someone whose name had been scratched away, said: *If you hear tiny wheels, do not follow them unless you are ready to be taken somewhere.*

I had worked here for four months when I discovered why these rules existed.

Until then, I assumed they were the sort of thing museum directors invented to make night guards feel important. The museum occupied the old east wing of the municipal library, a long brick building with ivy climbing the gutters and a roof that leaked whenever the wind came from the north. Its collection was modest by the standards of serious museums, but its strangeness was unmatched. I spent my first week repairing labels.

A bridge built halfway across a paper river. A brass key with “HOUSE NOT YET BUILT” engraved on the handle. A violin bow missing its final note. A cloud in a jar, supposedly captured during a school picnic in 1968. There was also an envelope containing a letter that began, “I know you will understand,” and ended, “If you receive this, please remember that the sky was blue that morning.”

The letter had never been sent. The museum’s founder, Evelyn Lark, had labeled it simply: *Some messages are completed by remaining unwritten.*

I liked that. I liked the deliberate punctuation, the small humility of it. Most objects in the museum had been donated by people who no longer knew what to do with them. Broken plans. Unused inheritances. Birthday presents still wrapped in paper from shops that had closed. Evelyn Lark had believed they deserved more careful descriptions than “miscellaneous.”

My job was to make sure visitors did not mistake the strange for the worthless. That mattered more than I could explain to the museum director, Martin Voss, who regarded our collection as a storage problem requiring expensive solutions.

“It’s a building,” Voss had told me during my interview, tapping the repair estimate on his desk. “Buildings can be insured.”

“It’s also a collection,” I said.

“Of unfinished things.”

“Exactly.”

Unfortunately, I said this while holding the cloud jar. I had not meant to argue for its preservation so passionately, but Voss had raised an eyebrow, and I spent the next twenty minutes defending objects that could not defend themselves. In the end, he gave me the job. I suspect he was relieved to have someone patient enough to answer complaints about the ghost in Room Seven.

The ghost in Room Seven was actually a draft. At least, that was what I told myself.

The night everything changed began with rain.

It was a Thursday in November, nearly two in the morning, when I heard a bell ring three times beneath the floor. I stopped halfway between the cloud jar and the key cabinet. The building was supposed to be empty. The heating system made sounds, pipes complained, rain worried the windows, but the old mechanical clock in the entrance hall had a voice like a bored man clearing his throat.

This was not that.

I walked into the hall.

The clock showed 12:14.

The clock also showed 12:14 when I checked my watch, which read 2:17. A label on the exhibition case near the door had come loose. It floated to the floor, turned over, and landed faceup.

The new label read: *THE LAST TRAIN IS ARRIVING.*

Behind me, something clicked.

I turned and saw the door to the model gallery open by itself. Inside, the paper bridge was trembling. Its little paper railings rattled. Its unfinished roadway lifted at one end and stretched toward the wall.

From the case marked *TRANSPORTATION OF UNCERTAIN DESTINATION*, a red toy train emerged.

It was no larger than my forearm. Its engine was painted with a black circle around the number 8. Behind it came three carriages, each carrying a wooden passenger. The fourth carriage was empty.

The train rolled across the floor without a sound.

Then, unmistakably, it began to whistle.

The sound was tiny, high, and impossible to ignore. I knew I should call Voss. I knew I should leave the building and wait for morning. Instead, I followed the train into the gallery.

The paper bridge had grown. It crossed the room in a gentle arc, no longer a model but something almost large enough to cross, its paper surface flexing beneath my shoes. The red train rolled onto it, and the wooden passengers swayed in their seats. The empty carriage waited at the bridge’s edge.

A figure unfolded itself from the timetable beside the display case. It was made of paper, though not cut from any ordinary page. Its head was round, its coat black, its cap marked with the same number as the train.

“Midnight service,” it said.

Its voice came from somewhere behind my ribs.

“Where does it go?”

“To wherever you meant to go.”

I looked at the empty carriage. “And if I’m not going anywhere?”

The conductor glanced at a pocket watch made of folded paper.

“Then you are delaying the timetable.”

From somewhere below us came the sound of wheels.

Not the train’s wheels. Many wheels. Tiny ones, clicking through corridors beneath the museum, rattling in distant rooms. The conductor turned toward the stairs.

“I recommend boarding,” it said.

Instead, I found myself looking at the painting in the far corner of the gallery.

I had passed it every night for four months. It showed a town beneath a pale sky, with white houses, a church steeple, and fields stretching toward blue hills. The title was *Larkfield at Dawn*. Larkfield had disappeared beneath a reservoir thirty years before the museum opened. The town existed now only in old photographs, drowned maps, and the memories of people who had been old enough to remember it.

In the painting, a girl was running along the road.

She stopped when she saw me.

Then she knocked on the frame.

I crossed the room. The paint had become warm beneath my fingers. The girl stood behind it, close enough that I could see the individual brushstrokes in her red scarf. She looked about ten years old.

“Can you open the way?” she called.

I looked at the gallery. The bridge had reached the wall and stopped.

“I don’t know how.”

“Find the key.”

“The key to a house that was never built?”

“That’s the one.”

Other things were happening now. The envelopes in the correspondence case had begun to flutter. The cloud in its jar rose slowly upward, pressing against the glass. A small paper figure climbed onto the bridge and waved at the train. The violin bow stood upright on a stand, pointing toward the ceiling.

I was beginning to understand that the rules had not been warnings. They were instructions for keeping the museum closed.

The girl in the painting watched the train depart.

“It comes every night,” she said. “Every night, it waits for someone to decide.”

“Decide what?”

“Whether they are going.”

Her expression was older than her face. The painted light shifted over the fields, and the road behind her filled with people carrying suitcases. They were leaving Larkfield. None of them looked back.

“I’m not a ghost,” she said, answering a question I had not asked. “I’m a possibility. The town this way, instead of the other. That is what the painter wanted to remember.”

I looked again at the water jar. The cloud inside it was not escaping. It was straining against the glass as if trying to become weather.

“For now.”

“Would you like to?”

She considered this. “I would like to be remembered. But being remembered is not the same as being rescued.”

I used the brass handle to lift the glass. The moment my fingers closed around it, something opened in the floor beneath my feet. A seam of blue light ran beneath the bridge, dividing the gallery from a narrow corridor I had never noticed.

The key had not opened a door. It had revealed one.

I found the corridor, the key, and the bridge in one night, and the next morning he found me asleep beneath the exhibition table with a brass key in my hand. He did not believe my story. He believed, however, in the bridge.

The paper structure had extended beneath the floor and emerged in the loading bay, where its unfinished end rested against the concrete wall. “Explain,” he said.

I told him about the train.

“The train is a toy.”

“I know.”

“The bridge is made of paper.”

“Mostly.”

He looked toward the loading bay. The bridge was trembling. A new line of blue light was traveling through its paper roadway.

“By whom?”

“By people who will want the space.”

He was a tired man in a wool coat, holding a clipboard and trying to preserve a building that no one had found worth preserving. He had not locked the doors to be cruel. He had simply stopped believing that the contents mattered.

The bridge snapped.

A piece of paper fell from the ceiling.

On the other side:

“The founder.”

We followed the blue seam beneath the floor. It passed through the gallery, then a storeroom, then a narrow passage behind the boiler. The walls were covered with pencil marks, some old, some fresh. At the end stood a door with no handle.

The key fitted the lock.

Beyond it was a round room with a skylight. A single plinth stood in the center. The rain had stopped, and the first gray light of morning was gathering above us.

On the plinth lay an old tape recorder.

A note was tied to its handle.

*Press play. Do not stop the recording.*

I pressed play.

Evelyn Lark’s voice filled the room.

“The Museum of Unfinished Things is not a museum of failure,” she said. Her voice sounded faint and dry, like paper being unfolded. “It is a museum of permission. Permission to change one’s mind. Voss looked at me. I looked at the recorder.

“Fix it.”

“Tomorrow,” I said.

I wrote a new label for the unopened letter:

I put the letter in an envelope, addressed it, and carried it to the postbox.

I took out a pen and added a sentence beneath it:

*If you hear tiny wheels, do not follow them. Unless you are ready to find your way back.*

I left the rule there for the next night guard.
